title: The Other Chair
description: You work in a mid-sized company navigating real workplace dilemmas — team meetings, performance conversations, project decisions. After each choice, the next round asks you to argue why the opposite choice was actually right. This is not about being contrarian. It is about learning to hold multiple valid models of the same situation simultaneously.
learning_concept: Cognitive flexibility — the ability to see a situation from multiple genuine perspectives — is one of the most trainable and most undervalued leadership skills. The Socratic method works not by finding the right answer but by discovering how many good answers exist simultaneously.
learning_objectives: Practice holding two competing perspectives on the same decision without dismissing either one as obviously wrong
Develop the skill of steelmanning — constructing the strongest possible argument for a position you did not choose
Understand how context, role, and information affect which perspective feels most 'correct' at any given moment
Build comfort with the discomfort of genuine ambiguity in complex workplace decisions

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Each odd-numbered round (1, 3, 5, 7) presents a real workplace dilemma. Choose what you would actually do.
Each even-numbered round (2, 4, 6) opens with a reference to your previous choice and asks you to argue why the opposite decision was right.
Round 7 is an integration round — you make a final choice while explicitly holding both perspectives you have developed.
Watch your two resources: Perspective Range (how many genuine viewpoints you can hold) and Cognitive Flex (how readily you shift between them).
The feedback on 'opposite argument' rounds validates that the other perspective has real merit — this is not a trick. Both positions are genuinely defensible.
tips: The hardest part of this game is the even rounds — resisting the urge to make a weak argument for the opposite side.
Steelmanning means constructing the best possible version of an argument you disagree with. It is a skill that takes practice.
Notice when 'arguing the other side' feels fake versus when it actually reveals something you had missed.
The goal is not to become a relativist who has no views. It is to hold your views with more precision and less rigidity.

psychological_framework.description: The game is built on three bodies of research: the Socratic method (the examined position is stronger than the unexamined one), Scott Page's diversity of thinking (teams with cognitive diversity consistently outperform teams of individually brilliant people), and Carol Dweck's research on belief malleability (people who believe their views can be updated make better long-term decisions). The devil's advocate rounds force the specific skill that most professionals never deliberately practice: taking the opposing view seriously enough to find its genuine strengths.

core_skills.name: Adaptability
core_skills.description: The ability to shift your mental model when new information or a new frame reveals something you had not previously seen.

core_skills.name: Empathy
core_skills.description: Understanding another person's perspective from the inside — including when their perspective leads them to a different but equally defensible decision.

core_skills.name: Strategic Thinking
core_skills.description: The capacity to see a situation from multiple levels simultaneously — the immediate choice, its downstream effects, and the underlying values that make different options feel correct to different people.

glossary_terms.definition: The practice of constructing the strongest possible version of an argument you disagree with — the opposite of a strawman, which is constructing the weakest.
glossary_terms.example: Instead of dismissing a colleague's objection as fear of change, asking: 'What is the most legitimate version of their concern? What are they protecting that actually matters?'
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Philosopher Daniel Dennett describes steelmanning as the highest form of critical thinking. It is also the foundation of effective negotiation, conflict resolution, and strategic planning — because you cannot outmaneuver a position you have not genuinely understood.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: The most effective trial lawyers spend as much time building the opposing counsel's case as their own — because understanding where the other case is strongest tells them exactly where to attack.

glossary_terms.definition: The executive function that allows you to shift your thinking between concepts, or consider multiple concepts simultaneously — as opposed to cognitive rigidity, which locks you into a single frame.
glossary_terms.example: Seeing a team conflict as simultaneously a communication failure, a structural problem, and a symptom of cultural values — rather than choosing just one explanation.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Research by Angela Duckworth and colleagues shows that cognitive flexibility is more predictive of long-term performance than IQ in complex, ambiguous roles. It can be trained — and the most effective training method is deliberate practice with perspective shifts under mild pressure, which is exactly what this game creates.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Jeff Bezos famously says he changes his mind when facts change. But most people conflate 'changing your mind' with weakness. Bezos' principle is about cognitive flexibility — holding positions loosely enough to update them, and firmly enough to act on them.

glossary_terms.definition: A model developed by Chris Argyris showing how humans move from raw data to conclusions through a series of assumptions, filters, and interpretations — often without realizing the steps they skipped.
glossary_terms.example: A team member's brief email response becomes: 'They are being passive-aggressive' → 'They do not respect me' → 'I need to address this in the next meeting.' Each step up the ladder added meaning that was not in the data.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: The ladder explains why two people can observe the exact same behavior and reach completely opposite conclusions. It also explains why the devil's advocate exercise is so valuable — it forces you back down the ladder to look at the data again before climbing it from a different direction.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: In medicine, experienced clinicians are taught to 'present the chart' without editorializing — because the editorializing that happens on the ladder of inference is a major source of diagnostic error.

halftime_config.reflection_question: You have just argued for the opposite of your first choice. Did making that argument reveal anything that actually changes your view? Or did it strengthen your original position? Either answer is valid — what matters is noticing.
halftime_config.custom_message: The hardest part of the game is still ahead. The integration rounds ask you to hold both perspectives at once and still make a decision.

rounds.title: The Team Meeting Problem
rounds.story:
You manage a team of eight. Your weekly team meetings have been running over by twenty to thirty minutes consistently for the last two months. The overruns happen because three of your team members — senior, respected, and genuinely valuable — regularly take discussions in directions that are important but not on the agenda. Other team members have started coming late or leaving early. The meeting costs roughly sixteen person-hours per week.

You have been thinking about two different responses. The first is to institute a strict timer and agenda, cutting off discussions when time expires and moving remaining topics to async channels. The second is to let the meetings continue as they are but make attendance optional beyond the first thirty minutes, allowing those who are done to leave.

Both approaches have real merit. Both have real costs. There is no obviously correct answer here.
rounds.goal: Choose your approach to the team meeting problem
rounds.coaching_moment: How you run meetings is a statement about what you value — discipline and efficiency, or emergence and trust. Neither value is wrong. The question is which one this team needs most right now.

choices.label: Institute a strict timer and agenda — protect everyone's time and focus the discussion
choices.feedback: Meetings become tighter and end on time. People who were arriving late start arriving on time. Two of the three frequent tangent-makers are frustrated — they feel managed, not trusted. One of them starts doing the off-agenda discussions in one-on-ones instead, which is actually more efficient. The other stops raising issues altogether. You gained discipline. You may have muted something important. The question for round 2: what did the timer actually protect, and what did it close off?

choices.label: Make the meeting attendance optional after 30 minutes — let people self-select into depth
choices.feedback: Four people consistently leave at the thirty-minute mark. Four stay. The four who stay are the team's most senior thinkers and the ones with the deepest involvement in ongoing issues. The conversations that happen in that second thirty minutes are genuinely valuable. But the four who leave are increasingly disconnected from decisions made in those extra minutes. You have created two tiers inside one meeting. The question for round 2: what does the optional departure signal about who gets heard and who does not?
choices.coaching_moment: Making something optional is a form of respecting autonomy. It is also a form of creating invisible hierarchies — the people who stay become the de facto decision-makers.

choices.label: Address the real issue directly — have a conversation with the three frequent tangent-makers
choices.feedback: You have a direct conversation with each of the three team members separately. Two of them immediately acknowledge the issue and suggest a dedicated thirty-minute 'open issues' slot at the end. The third reveals that the tangents are their way of raising concerns they do not feel safe raising directly. This was the information you needed. You redesign the meeting based on what you learned. The structural intervention was treating the symptom. The conversation was treating the cause.
choices.coaching_moment: Structural solutions are faster than relational ones. They are also often treating the symptom rather than the cause. The hard conversation is almost always the more direct path to the actual issue.

rounds.reflection_prompt: What meeting dynamics did you notice that the person running it probably couldn't see? What's the cost of those blind spots?

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: The Other Chair: Meeting Structure
rounds.story:
In the previous round, you chose an approach to the meeting problem. Now, step into the other chair.

If you chose the strict timer: you are now arguing that the optional-attendance or direct-conversation approach was actually the better choice. If you chose optional attendance: argue for the strict timer. If you chose the direct conversation: argue that structural solutions are more reliable than interpersonal ones.

This is not about changing your mind. It is about finding the genuine merit in what you did not choose. The argument you make here should be one you actually believe as you say it.
rounds.goal: Construct the strongest case for the approach you did not choose
rounds.coaching_moment: Steelmanning is not debating. It is truth-seeking. If you cannot find genuine merit in the opposite position, you probably have not understood it fully yet.
rounds.reflection_prompt: As you construct the argument for the other side: is there anything here that actually reveals a flaw in your original reasoning? Or does this exercise confirm that your original choice was right — for reasons you can now name more precisely?

choices.label: The timer approach is right because discipline and respect for time are themselves a form of care for the team
choices.feedback: A strong steelman. The argument that consistently overrunning meetings is a form of disrespect — of other people's time, their other commitments, their cognitive load — is completely valid. Some team members cannot advocate for themselves in the moment. The timer advocates for them. Structure is not the enemy of trust; unexamined informality can be its own form of favoritism. This argument has real weight. Does it change how you think about the choice you made?

choices.label: The optional approach is right because it treats adults as capable of determining their own time needs
choices.feedback: A strong steelman. Adult autonomy is a real value in team design. People who are forced to attend meetings they do not need to attend develop resentment that is far more corrosive than the inefficiency of a longer meeting. Optionality is a form of respect. The risk of tiering is real, but it can be managed through good meeting documentation. This argument holds. What does finding its merit tell you about the argument you actually made?

choices.label: The direct conversation is right because it treats the problem as fundamentally human, not structural
choices.feedback: An excellent steelman. The insight that structural solutions treat symptoms while relational solutions treat causes is one of the most important principles in organizational behavior. A timer does not tell you why someone keeps taking conversations off-agenda. A conversation might. The strongest argument for the direct conversation approach is that it is the only one that produces information — and information is what you actually need to make a lasting change.
choices.coaching_moment: The strongest steelman arguments are the ones that reveal an assumption you were holding in your original choice. What assumption does this opposite argument surface?

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: The Performance Review
rounds.story:
You are giving a performance review to Priya, a strong mid-level employee who has been with the company for three years. She is consistently good — reliable, technically skilled, well-liked — but she has not grown significantly in the past eighteen months. She has not taken on new challenges. She has not proactively sought new responsibilities. She does her job well and stops there.

You are about to give her an annual rating. Company policy has three options: Exceeds Expectations, Meets Expectations, or Below Expectations. Priya clearly meets expectations. The question is whether you rate her higher, to recognize her consistency and reliability — or exactly at her performance level, with direct feedback about the growth you are not seeing.

She is almost certainly expecting Exceeds. Almost everyone is.
rounds.goal: Choose how to rate and deliver Priya's performance review
rounds.coaching_moment: Feedback that prioritizes someone's comfort over their development is a form of kindness that costs them something real. But feedback delivered without the relationship to receive it is just criticism.

choices.label: Rate her Meets Expectations and have a direct, specific conversation about the growth gap
choices.feedback: Priya is visibly surprised and hurt. The conversation is difficult. You have done it with care — specific examples, no personal criticism, clear forward path — but it still lands as a rejection of effort she felt was real. She leaves the meeting quieter than she came in. In the weeks that follow, she either rises to the challenge or she starts looking for a new job. You will not know which for some time. The feedback was honest and specific. The relationship now depends on how you follow up.
choices.coaching_moment: Difficult honest feedback is an investment in someone's future that they may not be able to receive in the present. The manager's job is to make the feedback survivable, not comfortable.

choices.label: Rate her Exceeds Expectations — her consistency and reliability deserve recognition
choices.feedback: Priya is genuinely pleased. She thanks you warmly. You feel good in the room. But you have told her, through a rating, that what she is doing is more than enough — which means she has no reason to change. Next year the gap will be larger. And you will be giving her an Exceeds rating again or a much harder Meets Expectations — with eighteen more months of reinforced assumptions behind it. Short-term kindness, long-term cost.

choices.label: Rate her Meets Expectations but frame the growth feedback as opportunity, not criticism
choices.feedback: You lead with what is real: 'You are one of the most reliable people on this team and I want to be honest with you about where I see the next level of growth.' Priya takes the Meets rating hard initially but softens as the conversation becomes specific and generative. You end by asking her what she wants — not just what you want from her. She mentions two projects she has wanted to take on but thought were 'above her level.' You had not known. The conversation opened a door neither of you expected.

rounds.reflection_prompt: What emotions come up when you imagine being on the receiving end of the feedback you just gave?

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: The Other Chair: Performance Review
rounds.story:
In round 3, you chose how to handle Priya's performance review. Now step into the other chair.

If you chose the direct Meets rating with growth feedback: argue that rating her Exceeds was actually the right call. If you rated her Exceeds: argue for the direct Meets with growth feedback. If you chose the middle path: argue that one of the two more extreme options was actually more honest.

Make the best possible version of the argument. Find the genuine insight in the position you did not take.
rounds.goal: Argue for the performance review approach you did not choose
rounds.coaching_moment: The strongest steelman in this round will surface something uncomfortable: that the compassionate choice and the honest choice are both forms of care, and the line between them is not where you thought it was.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What does the strongest version of the opposite argument tell you about what you were actually weighing when you made your original choice? Was it Priya's development, your own comfort, your sense of what fairness means?

choices.label: Exceeds was right: reliability and consistency are exactly what organizations say they want and almost never reward
choices.feedback: A powerful steelman. The argument that companies systematically undervalue reliable, consistent performers in favor of flashy, high-variability ones is well-supported by organizational research. Priya's consistency IS a form of excellence. The rating system may be the problem, not Priya's behavior. This argument genuinely challenges the assumption that 'growth' always means taking on more scope — rather than doing what you do with increasing mastery. What does finding this merit reveal about your original reasoning?

choices.label: The direct Meets rating was right: inflated ratings are a systemic problem that harms everyone, including Priya
choices.feedback: A strong steelman. Rating inflation is one of the most documented and damaging practices in corporate performance management. When everyone receives Exceeds, the rating loses meaning. Priya is harmed by being given a rating that is not credible — it tells her she is excellent when the market and the company's actual expectations say otherwise. Honest ratings, across the board, are a form of institutional respect. This argument is real. Does it change how you think about what you did?

choices.label: The middle path was right: the rating matters less than the conversation, and the conversation could have been had regardless of the number
choices.feedback: A nuanced steelman. The argument that the conversation about growth should be decoupled from the rating — that it should happen consistently regardless of whether the rating is Meets or Exceeds — has real merit. The rating is a number. The relationship is where the change happens. Making the growth conversation contingent on the rating creates a structure where employees only receive honest developmental feedback when they are underperforming. That is exactly backwards. What does this reveal about the current design of performance management?

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: The Project Scope Decision
rounds.story:
Your team has been working for six weeks on a product feature — a customer dashboard redesign. You are eight days from the planned release. Your lead designer surfaces a problem: a new user research session yesterday revealed that the navigation structure you have built does not work for power users. It is fine for casual users. But power users — your highest-value customer segment — will be slowed down by it.

You have three options. Ship as planned and patch it post-launch. Delay the launch by two weeks to address the power user issue properly. Or launch a simplified version that excludes the advanced navigation and add it in the next sprint.

All three options have legitimate cases. Which do you choose?
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle the pre-launch scope problem
rounds.coaching_moment: Ship-it-and-fix-it culture values speed and momentum. Fix-it-before-it-ships culture values quality and user trust. Neither is universally correct. The right answer depends on who your users are and what they have come to expect from you.

choices.label: Ship as planned — get user feedback at scale and patch the power user issue post-launch
choices.feedback: Launch happens on time. Casual users love the redesign. Three power users file detailed bug reports within forty-eight hours. Your account manager flags that two of them are at renewal — and both mentioned the navigation issue in their check-in calls this week. The patch is ready in twelve days. Those twelve days cost something that is hard to calculate: trust from your highest-value segment, built over months, partially eroded in less than two weeks. Was the eight-day difference worth it?

choices.label: Delay two weeks — fix the power user issue properly before anyone encounters it
choices.feedback: The delay costs you two weeks of timeline and a difficult conversation with the stakeholder who was expecting the launch. But the version that ships has solid navigation for both user types. No bug reports on navigation. Power users complete their first session without friction. The stakeholder who was most frustrated about the delay sends you a note after launch: 'Good call on the delay.' Not everyone will say that in the moment. Some will only say it afterwards.
choices.coaching_moment: The cost of delay is visible on a timeline. The cost of shipping something broken to high-value users is invisible until it is too late. One is countable; the other is not. That asymmetry drives most ship-it-now decisions.

choices.label: Launch a simplified version for all users now and add the power user navigation in the next sprint
choices.feedback: You ship a version that works cleanly for both segments — just with less advanced navigation than originally planned. Power users accept this as a phased release. Casual users do not notice the difference. The next sprint adds the full navigation feature. The overall timeline is extended by three weeks versus the delay approach, but the launch itself lands without trust damage. This is the creative third option — reframing the binary as a sequencing question rather than a go/no-go.

rounds.reflection_prompt: When you switch chairs, which parts of the scope decision feel very different — and what does that reveal about perspective?

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: The Other Chair: Scope Decision
rounds.story:
In round 5, you chose how to handle the pre-launch scope problem. Now, step into the other chair.

If you shipped as planned: argue that delaying was the right call. If you delayed: argue for shipping and patching post-launch. If you went with the simplified version: argue that one of the other two approaches was more honest or more effective.

The strongest argument here will acknowledge the real costs of your original choice — not just the benefits of the alternative. Steelmanning is not cheerleading for the other side. It is finding the genuine insight you missed.
rounds.goal: Argue the strongest case for the approach you did not choose
rounds.coaching_moment: Notice which arguments are easy to make and which feel dishonest to say out loud. The discomfort of making a genuine argument for the other side is where the learning lives.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Does making this argument change your view of the choice you made in round 5? If not, can you identify precisely what the opposite argument misses that your original reasoning accounted for?

choices.label: Shipping was right: iteration is the only way to learn at scale, and perfecting before launch is a form of arrogance
choices.feedback: A strong steelman. The argument that you cannot predict user behavior from a research session — that the only valid test is at scale, in production, with real users under real conditions — is a foundational principle of modern product development. User research is a signal, not a certainty. Shipping and learning is sometimes more respectful of users than delaying to perfect something based on what you think they need. This argument is real. Does it land?

choices.label: Delaying was right: trust with high-value users is a strategic asset that cannot be rebuilt cheaply once damaged
choices.feedback: A strong steelman. The argument that customer trust, especially from high-value power users, is a strategic asset with extremely high rebuild cost is well-supported by customer success research. The marginal cost of a two-week delay is knowable and bounded. The cost of eroding trust with your highest-LTV segment is neither knowable nor bounded — and it compounds over time. This argument is correct. How does it interact with the arguments for the other side?

choices.label: The simplified launch was right: reframing binary decisions into sequencing questions is always better than the original framing
choices.feedback: An excellent steelman — and in this case, genuinely the most sophisticated argument. The meta-insight is that the original framing of the problem as ship-vs-delay was itself the constraint that needed to be challenged. The best decision-makers do not just evaluate the options presented; they examine whether the options are the right options. Reframing binary decisions into sequencing questions is a cognitive move, not just a practical one. It requires the flexibility to step outside the frame entirely.

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: The Integration Round
rounds.story:
Across the last six rounds, you have made three real decisions and argued for the opposite in each case. You have found genuine merit in positions you did not originally choose. You have (maybe) noticed that your certainty about your own choices changed slightly, or that your ability to understand why someone would choose differently has grown.

Now, a final scenario — the integration round. Your company is deciding whether to implement a mandatory 360-degree feedback process, where every employee receives upward, downward, and peer feedback twice a year. Some people strongly support it: more information, more accountability, better development. Some people strongly oppose it: feedback without trust is just surveillance, and formal processes tend to formalize the wrong things.

You are on the committee making this recommendation. You have one vote. You have now spent this game practicing how to hold two genuine perspectives at once.

What do you actually recommend?
rounds.goal: Make a final recommendation while holding both perspectives
rounds.coaching_moment: The goal of cognitive flexibility is not to have no views. It is to hold your views with precision — knowing exactly what they are based on, what they are vulnerable to, and where a genuinely different view has merit you cannot dismiss.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Before you vote: what is the most legitimate argument against the position you are about to choose? Can you name it clearly? If you can, your recommendation is a real one. If you cannot, you may still be inside the original framing.

choices.label: Recommend the 360 process — structured feedback is better than the informal feedback most people never receive
choices.feedback: You vote yes — but you have a specific condition: the process needs to be built with psychological safety at its center, not accountability at its center. You recommend pairing the 360 with training on how to give and receive feedback before the process launches. You have held the opposite argument — that formalization without trust is surveillance — and you have incorporated it into a yes vote that is more sophisticated than a simple yes. That is what cognitive flexibility produces: better decisions with clearer foundations.
choices.coaching_moment: A recommendation that incorporates the strongest objection to itself is more trustworthy than one that ignores it. Cognitive flexibility does not produce wishy-washy positions — it produces more precisely reasoned ones.

choices.label: Recommend against the 360 process — the conditions for feedback to work do not yet exist here
choices.feedback: You vote no — but with a specific alternative: you recommend a six-month investment in psychological safety culture first, followed by a pilot 360 process with a small team who opt in. You have held the opposite argument — that people who lack formal feedback may be developing blind spots that hurt them and the organization — and you have incorporated it into a no vote that is not dismissive but sequenced. You are not against feedback. You are against feedback without the soil it needs to grow. That nuance is what made this a real decision.

choices.label: Abstain and request more data — the committee needs information about the team's current feedback culture before deciding
choices.feedback: You propose a diagnostic first: a confidential pulse survey measuring the team's current relationship to feedback — how safe they feel giving it, how often they receive it informally, what they believe about the current culture. You have recognized that both the yes and the no arguments are built on assumptions about the organization's current state that no one on the committee has actually verified. The decision to gather information before deciding is itself a decision — one that requires the cognitive flexibility to step outside the existing framing entirely and ask a different question.

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

transfer_exercises.game_context: Arguing for the opposite of your choice in rounds 2, 4, and 6
transfer_exercises.real_world: This week, find one position you hold firmly — about a work decision, a person's behavior, or a policy — and spend five minutes constructing the strongest possible case against it. Write it down. Notice what it feels like when the counter-argument is genuinely good.
transfer_exercises.challenge: In your next disagreement with a colleague, before responding to their position, spend sixty seconds trying to understand it from the inside. What are they protecting? What would you need to believe for their position to seem obviously correct?

transfer_exercises.game_context: The integration round — making a recommendation while holding both perspectives
transfer_exercises.real_world: The next time you are making a recommendation — at work, at home, in a group — include one sentence in your recommendation that names the strongest objection to your own position. Notice whether this makes you sound less decisive or more credible.
transfer_exercises.challenge: Find a decision your organization recently made that you disagreed with. Spend fifteen minutes writing the strongest possible argument for why the decision was correct. If you can find genuine merit in it, what does that tell you about the original disagreement?

achievements.name: The Steelman
achievements.description: In all three devil's advocate rounds, chose the option that most genuinely engaged with the opposite position rather than offering a weak or dismissive counter-argument.

achievements.name: Both Chairs
achievements.description: Finished the game with Perspective Range above 70 — demonstrating a sustained ability to hold multiple genuine perspectives across all 7 rounds.

achievements.name: Precise Thinker
achievements.description: In the integration round, chose an option that incorporated the strongest objection to itself — demonstrating that cognitive flexibility produces sharper, not softer, positions.

cultural_context: Leadership development is a core focus of India's leading business schools and corporate training programmes. The Other Chair develops the situational judgement and team management skills that India's organisations need at every level.
coaching_moment: Every choice shapes your strategy — great leaders think several steps ahead before deciding.
reflection_prompt: Which decision in this run shifted your outcome the most? What signal told you it was the right call?
